text.p: Copper prices stepped back from their highs during Wednesday afternoon LME trading, but still closed steadier as did most of the metals complex. However, the pace of trade in all markets was slow, with the next major move difficult to discern now that the investment funds have stepped aside for the moment.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index ended 1.26 points higher at 241.24.

On the LME, copper prices performed adequately throughout after recapturing $2,300 with stocks falling 5,350 tonnes due to drawdowns in Singapore and Hamburg. But the market stalled just above $2,310 and settled back on the kerb to close at $2,307, a net gain of $15 from Tuesday.

Aluminium flipped up to a high-point of $1,597 during the kerb, when buy-stops were triggered above the $1,590 level -- an area where 100-day moving average resistance was pegged. Last trade was at $1,592, up $9.50 from Tuesday.

Nickel prices reached a high water-mark of $7,500 in mid-afternoon trading before backtracking from this important chart objective. Despite some stern selling at this level the market nevertheless maintained a strong technical bounce from Monday's lows. Traders said the market is in limbo on the charts, but could well subside back to levels nearer $7,100. Last trade was at $7,490, up $185 from the previous kerb.

Zinc business was fairly routine thoughout the session, with a generally steadier trend a reflection of a 2,075-tonne stock decline. Prices movements were thin, however, and last trade was at $1,266, up $6.
The lead market saw little interest and as a consequence hardly budged during the day. There was a modest dip towards $650, but last business at $652 was just $1 down from Tuesday.
Tin business was equally uninspiring, with the market gradually edging up from overnight levels to end at $5,760, a $20 advance. The alloy market was marked up fractionally to $1,475/1,480 a tonne.

CBOT wheat futures closed higher on bullish input from the export sector and on jitters about cold weather in portions of the U.S. winter wheat growing region, traders said. Wheat closed unchanged to 3-1/2 cents per bushel higher, with May up 3-1/2 at $3.85-1/2.

NYMEX crude ended lower Wednesday after bullish oil inventory data failed to extend early session gains, allowing the oil market to slip back into a bearish mode. "There was an API reversal that has been typical in the past couple weeks, so we are back to seeing lower lows made in late session, which indicates how bearish the market is," said Sal Gugliara of United Energy in New York. May crude ended off eight cents to $19.27 a barrel after rising as high as $19.77.

COMEX gold and silver futures ended lower Wednesday, but NYMEX platinum and palladium rose for the third session in a row, as the disruption to Russian supplies again began to be felt, traders said. June gold ended down 80 cents at $350.50 an ounce, but is still seen trapped in its $348.30-358.00 range of the past month. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $347.80/30 compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $347.80 and the New York close Tuesday around $348.30/80.
